analysis.subject: physics
analysis.pageCoverage: Page introduces simplified motion where opposing forces balance for steady level flight, explains Newton second law relating net force mass and acceleration, and describes rise fall accelerate and slow outcomes when lift weight or thrust drag become unbalanced

overview.headline: Balanced flight and how unbalanced forces create aircraft motion

keyPoints.point: Simplified flight studies one force direction while some other forces stay balanced
keyPoints.quote: some of the four forces acting on the aircraft are balanced by other forces

keyPoints.point: Steady level flight keeps weight balanced by lift and drag balanced by thrust
keyPoints.quote: the weight would be balanced by the lift and the drag would be balanced by the thrust

keyPoints.point: Unbalanced forces make the aircraft move in the direction of the greater force
keyPoints.quote: If the forces become unbalanced, the aircraft will move in the direction of the greater force.

keyPoints.point: Net force equals the difference between opposing forces such as lift minus weight and thrust minus drag
keyPoints.quote: The net force is the difference between the opposing forces; lift minus weight, or thrust minus drag.

keyTerms.gloss: gravitational pull balanced by lift in level flight
keyTerms.quote: the weight would be balanced by the lift and the drag would be balanced by the thrust

keyTerms.gloss: upward force held constant to sustain flight against weight
keyTerms.quote: If the weight is decreased while the lift is held constant, the airplane will rise:

keyTerms.gloss: forward propulsive force that can be constant while increasing thrust causes acceleration
keyTerms.quote: Similarly, increasing the thrust while the drag is constant will cause the plane to accelerate:

keyTerms.gloss: resistive force acting opposite thrust that at constant value causes aircraft to slow
keyTerms.quote: And increasing the drag at a constant thrust will cause the plane to slow down:

keyTerms.gloss: change in velocity produced by net force acting on aircraft
keyTerms.quote: Where a is the acceleration, m is the mass of the aircraft, and F is the net force acting on the aircraft.
